questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Ratings move only once a year
questions.question: Over the past year, an insurer made three major system changes and had two serious incidents, yet its risk ratings changed only at the annual review. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Move the register review from yearly to quarterly
options.B: Ask internal audit to assess the ratings each year
options.C: Link change and incident processes to reassessment
options.D: Add staff to the risk team for the annual review

questions.key_concept: Material changes, incidents and breaches should trigger reassessment through links to change and incident processes, with scheduled reviews as a backstop.
questions.pre_read: Ask what should have caused the ratings to move between reviews.
questions.correct_explanation: Major changes and serious incidents are triggers: each can shift likelihood or impact the day it happens. Linking change management and incident processes to the risk function makes each trigger start a reassessment, so ratings move when risk moves. Moving to quarterly reviews narrows the gap, but a change made the week after a review still waits up to three months, and the review stays tied to the calendar rather than the event.

wrong_explanations.A: Quarterly reviews narrow the gap, but ratings still wait for the calendar rather than moving when a change or incident happens.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance on the process; it does not maintain ratings, and a yearly review keeps the same delay.
wrong_explanations.D: More staff make the annual review thorough, but ratings still go a year without reflecting changes and incidents.

tips: Eliminate: B hands rating work that belongs to management and the risk function to internal audit, and D strengthens the annual review without shortening the delay.
Final two: C beats A because triggers move ratings when risk moves; a quarterly calendar is still a calendar.
Exam cue: material change, serious incidents and threshold breaches trigger reassessment; look for options tied to the event, not the date.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Ending scheduled reviews
questions.question: An airport operator now starts a risk reassessment on every major change, incident and threshold breach, and its CIO proposes ending scheduled risk reviews. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: End the scheduled reviews and rely on the triggers
options.B: Pass the scheduled reviews to internal audit
options.C: Keep scheduled reviews alongside the triggers
options.D: Keep scheduled reviews for the ten highest risks

questions.key_concept: Triggers catch change that someone records; scheduled reviews stay as a backstop for change nobody reports, at a frequency set by risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a trigger depends on to fire, and what happens when that does not occur.
questions.correct_explanation: Triggers fire only when someone records a change, incident or breach; drift, unreported changes and slow shifts in threats pass them by. Scheduled reviews remain the backstop, with frequency set by each risk's rating. Keeping them for the ten highest risks saves effort, but it leaves every other risk without a backstop, even though an unreported change can turn a low-rated risk into a serious one.

wrong_explanations.A: Triggers depend on someone recording the event; without scheduled reviews, unreported change and gradual drift are never picked up.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; running the risk function's reviews would compromise that independence and take them away from the function that maintains the ratings.
wrong_explanations.D: Limiting reviews to the top ten leaves lower-rated risks with no backstop, though unreported change can raise them.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes triggers catch every change, and B hands a risk-function task to internal audit, whose role is independent assurance.
Final two: C beats D because unreported change can affect any risk; keep a backstop for all of them, with frequency set by rating.
Exam cue: event triggers and scheduled reviews work together; an option that drops either one is the trap.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Asked to fill in a self-assessment
questions.question: A bank's payments division head asks the risk team to complete the division's control self-assessment on its managers' behalf, to save them time. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Run a short workshop where managers rate their controls
options.B: Complete the assessment and have each manager sign it
options.C: Ask internal audit to complete the assessment this year
options.D: Defer the division's assessment to next year's cycle

questions.key_concept: In control self-assessment the risk function designs and facilitates while managers rate their own controls; doing it for them loses the ownership it builds.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose knowledge and ownership a self-assessment is meant to capture.
questions.correct_explanation: Control self-assessment works because the managers who run the controls judge them, which builds first-line ownership. The risk team designs the questions and facilitates, and a short workshop respects the managers' time while keeping the ratings theirs. Completing it for them and collecting signatures looks efficient, but the ratings become the risk team's views, signed by managers who may never have examined their own controls.

wrong_explanations.B: Ratings written by the risk team are second-line opinions under first-line names; the ownership self-assessment exists to build is lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance; completing management's self-assessment would compromise that role and still remove manager ownership.
wrong_explanations.D: Deferring leaves the division's controls unassessed for a year and does not address the managers' time concern.

tips: Eliminate: C has the third line do management's self-assessment, and D leaves the division unassessed without solving the time problem.
Final two: A beats B because the managers must make the ratings; signatures on the risk team's answers keep the form but lose the ownership.
Exam cue: in self-assessment the second line facilitates and challenges; the first line assesses its own controls.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. 600 checks ready to switch on
questions.question: A medical device maker has bought a continuous monitoring platform with 600 ready-made checks, and IT plans to switch them all on next week. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Turn on the 600 checks now and tune out noise later
options.B: Route the alerts to the CISO's team for review
options.C: Enable the checks the platform vendor marks as critical
options.D: Start with checks on controls over the top risks

questions.key_concept: A monitoring strategy decides what to monitor first, how often and who acts, starting with the controls behind the highest risks.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens the week after 600 checks start sending results to people.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring helps only when someone acts on its results. Starting with checks on the controls behind the top risks, each with an owner and response time, builds a strategy tied to risk tolerance and keeps alerts manageable. Turning everything on and tuning later promises full coverage, but floods teams with alerts before anyone knows which matter, so real warnings get lost while tuning catches up.

wrong_explanations.A: Full coverage on day one buries the important alerts in noise; alert fatigue sets in before tuning reaches the checks that matter.
wrong_explanations.B: One team receiving every alert becomes a bottleneck; alerts should reach the owners who can act on each control.
wrong_explanations.C: The vendor's critical label reflects generic threats, not which controls guard this maker's top risks.

tips: Eliminate: B funnels the alerts to one team instead of the owners who act, and C lets the vendor's labels, not the maker's risks, decide what to monitor.
Final two: D beats A because a risk-based start keeps alerts actionable; switching everything on and tuning later invites alert fatigue.
Exam cue: monitoring follows a strategy: controls behind the top risks first, an owner for each alert, frequency set by risk.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. One score from the heat map
questions.question: The board asks a payment firm's risk analyst for one overall IT risk score, computed by averaging the 1 to 25 heat-map scores of its 60 risks. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Provide the full table of the 60 risk scores
options.B: Offer the profile of risks against appetite and trend
options.C: Weight the average by each risk's impact score
options.D: Average the scores of the risks above appetite

questions.key_concept: Heat-map scores are ordinal, so averaging them misleads; the board gets the risk profile against appetite, with trend.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether a heat-map score of 12 is really twice as bad as a score of 6.
questions.correct_explanation: Heat-map scores rank risks but are not true quantities, so averaging them, weighted or not, produces a number with no clear meaning that can hide a single critical risk. The analyst offers what the board needs to decide: the profile of risks against appetite, with trend. Weighting the average by impact sounds more rigorous, but it adds more arithmetic on ordinal scores and still blends many risks into one figure.

wrong_explanations.A: The full table gives the board detail without the view against appetite it needs; boards want the profile, not every score.
wrong_explanations.C: Weighting adds more arithmetic on ordinal scores; the result still has no clear meaning and still blends risks together.
wrong_explanations.D: Averaging the worst risks still hides which one is furthest above appetite, the fact the board most needs.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the board detail instead of the profile against appetite, and D averages the very risks the board needs to see one by one.
Final two: B beats C because ordinal scores cannot be meaningfully averaged, weighted or not; the board needs the profile against appetite.
Exam cue: do not add, average or weight heat-map scores; report the profile against appetite, with trend, to the board.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Bare numbers on a dashboard
questions.question: A telecom's dashboard for its executive committee shows each KRI's current value as a bare number. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend adding as MOST important?

options.A: The underlying records behind each KRI value
options.B: A single overall score combining the KRIs
options.C: Each KRI's thresholds and its recent trend
options.D: Each KRI's value compared with industry averages

questions.key_concept: A KRI value means little alone; thresholds tied to tolerance and the recent trend show whether exposure is acceptable and which way it is moving.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an executive would need to know whether a value of 37 is good or bad.
questions.correct_explanation: A number on its own does not say whether exposure is acceptable or worsening. Thresholds drawn from tolerance show where each KRI sits against the agreed limits, and the recent trend shows direction, so the committee sees what needs a decision. Industry averages add context and tempt, but peers' figures were not set from this telecom's tolerance, so a KRI can beat the average and still breach the company's own limit.

wrong_explanations.A: Underlying records help validate the data, but executives need context to decide, not raw detail.
wrong_explanations.B: Combining unrelated KRIs into one score hides which risk is moving and can mask a single breach.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer averages are not this company's tolerance; a KRI can look better than peers while still beyond the agreed limit.

tips: Eliminate: A gives executives raw detail instead of context, and B blends unrelated indicators into one score that masks which risk is moving.
Final two: C beats D because thresholds come from the company's own tolerance; peer averages say nothing about its limits.
Exam cue: report indicators against their thresholds and trend; a bare value or a peer comparison does not tell leaders when to act.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Same pack for every owner
questions.question: Each quarter, a risk analyst sends all 15 of a manufacturer's risk owners the same 40-page enterprise risk report, and few act on it. What is the analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Add a one-page summary to the front of the report
options.B: Send each owner a report on their own risks and actions
options.C: Ask the CEO to require each owner to read the report
options.D: Send the same 40-page report monthly instead of quarterly

questions.key_concept: Reports are built for the audience's decisions: each risk owner needs their own risks, indicators and actions due, not the enterprise pack.
questions.pre_read: Ask what one risk owner needs to see to know what to do next.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk owners act on their own risks, indicator status, overdue actions and acceptances due for review. A report built around each owner's portfolio puts those in front of them, so what needs action is clear. A one-page summary makes the enterprise report easier to read, but it summarizes the whole enterprise, so each owner still has to hunt through the pages for their own items.

wrong_explanations.A: A summary helps readers of the enterprise view, but it is still not organized around each owner's risks and due actions.
wrong_explanations.C: Pressure from the CEO may get the report read, but owners still have to dig through 40 pages for their own items.
wrong_explanations.D: Sending a report that does not fit its readers more often adds volume without making it more useful.

tips: Eliminate: C pushes owners to read a report that does not fit them, and D sends the same unsuitable report more often.
Final two: B beats A because each owner needs their own risks and actions; a summary still describes the whole enterprise.
Exam cue: match the report to its reader's decisions: boards get the profile against appetite, owners get their risks and actions.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Committee notes a risk without acting
questions.question: After a risk analyst presents a rising card-fraud risk to an e-commerce firm's executive committee, members note the risk and move to the next item without acting. Which addition would BEST improve the next report?

options.A: The decision needed, with options and their target risk
options.B: The risk's trend against its KRI thresholds over time
options.C: Technical detail of how the fraud attacks are carried out
options.D: A comparison of the firm's fraud losses with its peers

questions.key_concept: A report that asks for action states the decision requested, the options and what each would leave, so leaders can decide.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the committee already knew and what it did next.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee already knows the risk is rising; nothing in the report asked it for a decision. Stating the decision needed, with the response options and the target risk each would leave, turns the report into something it can act on. Trend against thresholds strengthens the case that action is due, but it repeats what the committee has already heard, that the risk is rising, without saying what to decide.

wrong_explanations.B: Trend against thresholds shows the risk is rising, which the committee already heard; it still does not say what decision is needed.
wrong_explanations.C: Attack detail suits the fraud team; executives need the decision and its options, not how the fraud works.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer comparison adds context, but it does not tell the committee what it is being asked to approve.

tips: Eliminate: C gives executives technical detail meant for specialists, and D offers context without saying what to decide.
Final two: A beats B because the committee's gap is the decision, not more evidence that the risk is rising; state the decision and its options.
Exam cue: reports to leaders end with the decision requested and the options, not just the problem.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Hundreds of signals a month
questions.question: A risk analyst's monthly horizon scan for an energy network operator returns about 300 signals from news, vendor alerts, research and regulators. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Screen the signals for relevance to the operator's objectives
options.B: Record each signal in the register as an emerging risk
options.C: Narrow the scan to alerts from government agencies
options.D: Pass the signals to unit heads to check against their objectives

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning feeds the register only after signals are screened for relevance to the enterprise's objectives and assets.
questions.pre_read: Ask how many of the 300 signals are likely to matter to this business.
questions.correct_explanation: Most signals will not matter to this operator. The analyst first screens them against its objectives, assets and operations, then raises the relevant ones as emerging risks with proposed owners. Passing the signals to unit heads uses their knowledge of their objectives, but sending them hundreds of unfiltered items each month buries the few that matter and pushes the risk function's screening work onto them.

wrong_explanations.B: Recording every signal floods the register with items that have nothing to do with the business and buries the few that do.
wrong_explanations.C: Narrowing the sources misses signals from research, vendors and regulators, where many emerging risks first appear.
wrong_explanations.D: Unit heads know their objectives, but hundreds of unfiltered signals each month bury the relevant ones and shift the screening onto them.

tips: Eliminate: B records every signal as a risk without screening, and C narrows the sources, losing signals from research, vendors and regulators.
Final two: A beats D because the risk function screens first; passing hundreds of unfiltered signals to unit heads buries what matters.
Exam cue: scan widely, then screen against objectives before recording; relevance comes before the register.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. New evidence on a deepfake risk
questions.question: A bank's risk analyst recorded deepfake voice fraud on payment approvals as an emerging risk with a wide rating range; peer losses and control tests now provide solid data. What is the analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Keep it as emerging with a shorter review date
options.B: Close the entry and record the control test results
options.C: Rate it critical from the peer banks' losses
options.D: Rate it on the usual scale in the main profile

questions.key_concept: An emerging risk moves into the main profile, rated on the usual scale, once evidence is good enough to rate it with confidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what made the risk 'emerging' in the first place, and whether that is still true.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk is held as emerging while too little is known to rate it normally. Peer losses and the bank's own control tests now provide that evidence, so the analyst rates it on the usual scale and moves it into the main profile, where it is compared with appetite and owned like any other risk. Keeping it emerging with a shorter review date suits real uncertainty, which the new data has now resolved.

wrong_explanations.A: Short reviews suit a risk that is still poorly understood; with solid data available, keeping it emerging delays a normal rating and response.
wrong_explanations.B: A tested control can lower the risk but does not remove it; closing the entry drops a live risk from the register.
wrong_explanations.C: Peer losses are evidence, but the rating should come from the bank's own likelihood, impact and controls, not from alarm.

tips: Eliminate: B removes a risk because one control was tested, and C rates it critical from peer losses rather than the bank's own analysis.
Final two: D beats A because the uncertainty that justified 'emerging' is gone; with solid data, rate it normally in the main profile.
Exam cue: emerging risks are refined as evidence grows and move into the main profile once they can be rated with confidence.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Owner for an AI shopping risk
questions.question: A risk analyst at an online grocer records AI shopping agents that buy for customers as an emerging risk to online sales. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate owner to propose?

options.A: The grocer's chief information officer
options.B: The risk team, as the function that recorded it
options.C: An owner named once the risk can be rated
options.D: The director of the online sales channel

questions.key_concept: An emerging risk gets a business owner while it is still uncertain: the manager whose objectives it affects, not IT or the risk team.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose objectives these agents would help or harm.
questions.correct_explanation: Even while uncertain, an emerging risk needs an owner who will watch it and decide on responses as evidence grows. AI agents buying for customers affect online sales, so the director of that channel owns the risk. Having the risk team that recorded it hold the risk sounds natural, but the practitioner advises and monitors; holding the risk would leave no business decision-maker watching it while it develops.

wrong_explanations.A: The CIO may support the technology work, but the risk is to online sales, a business objective owned by the channel's director.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk team records, analyzes and monitors; recording a risk does not make it the owner, and it leaves no business decision-maker in charge.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting to name an owner until the risk can be rated is the trap; emerging risks need an owner early, with their uncertainty stated.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a business risk to IT because AI is technology, and C delays naming an owner until the risk can be rated.
Final two: D beats B because the practitioner advises and monitors but does not own risk; the channel's director owns the objective at stake.
Exam cue: AI and emerging risks are owned by the business whose objectives they affect, from the day they are recorded.
